Under Article 53 of the EU AI Act, providers of general-purpose AI models must maintain technical documentation, make it available to authorities and downstream providers, establish a copyright policy, and publish a public summary of training data; open-source GPAI models are exempt from some documentation requirements unless classified as systemic-risk models.
The EU AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024, with Chapter V outlining GPAI provider obligations.

From 2 August 2025, obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models under the EU AI Act entered into application/application began, requiring compliance by providers placing GPAI models on the EU market after that date.
Providers of GPAI models with systemic risk must notify the EU AI Office without delay.
Providers who sign the EU GPAI Code of Practice signal intent to comply and receive streamlined compliance treatment, with Commission enforcement focusing on monitoring adherence to the code.
On 1 August 2025, the EU AI Office and the Board published their assessment of the adequacy of the final GPAI Code of Practice and invited providers to adhere to it.

The GPAI Code of Practice's Safety and Security chapter includes measures such as requiring systemic-risk model providers to include aggregate forecasts of when models may exceed the highest systemic risk tier.
In January 2025, Executive Order 14110 (Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of AI) was rescinded/repealed in the United States.

On July 23, 2025, the Trump Administration released 'Winning the Race: America's AI Action Plan,' a non-binding federal policy framework of more than 90 actions across three pillars: Accelerating Innovation, Building American AI Infrastructure, and Leading in International Diplomacy and Security.

The America's AI Action Plan was accompanied by executive orders including Promoting the Export of American AI Technology Stack, Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Infrastructure, and Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government.
The America's AI Action Plan recommends that NIST revise the AI Risk Management Framework to eliminate references to misinformation, Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion, and climate change.

On December 11, 2025, President Trump issued an Executive Order titled 'Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence,' aimed at establishing a uniform, minimally burdensome federal AI standard and directing development of federal legislation to preempt the patchwork of state AI laws, with limited exceptions such as child safety protections.

On June 2, 2026, President Trump signed a new Executive Order, 'Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security,' establishing cybersecurity mandates and a voluntary framework for secure deployment of frontier AI models.

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) is a voluntary framework for managing AI risk, not a binding regulatory requirement, and has continued to be updated through 2025-2026 with new profiles (e.g., agentic AI) without a formal 'AI RMF 2.0' release.

As of 2026, the EU enforces a horizontal, risk-tiered AI statute across member states, while US federal AI policy is combined with a fast-moving patchwork of state AI laws rather than a single binding federal AI statute.

Unlike the EU AI Act's binding legal obligations for GPAI/foundation model providers, current U.S. federal AI policy relies on executive orders, voluntary frameworks (e.g., NIST AI RMF), and action plans rather than enacted statutory requirements specific to foundation models.

A CSIS analysis (through June 2026) compares U.S. state frontier AI bills to the EU AI Act and voluntary industry frameworks, finding that the most pro-regulatory state AI bills have failed to gain traction while more modest approaches have had more success.

report:
# EU AI Act Foundation Model Requirements vs. US Federal AI Policy: A Comparative Analysis

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act imposes binding, legally enforceable obligations on providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models, particularly those deemed to pose "systemic risk," including documentation, transparency, and risk-mitigation duties ([EU Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/general-purpose-ai-models-ai-act-questions-answers)). By contrast, US federal AI policy as of late 2025/2026 remains a shifting assemblage of executive orders and voluntary frameworks without a binding statutory equivalent for foundation models ([Sidley Austin](https://www.sidley.com/en/insights/newsupdates/2025/12/unpacking-the-december-11-2025-executive-order), [ailawsbystate.com](https://www.ailawsbystate.com/blog/eu-ai-act-vs-us-state-ai-laws-comparison)). This creates a structural asymmetry: the EU enforces a harmonized, risk-tiered legal regime, while the US approach is fragmented across federal executive action and state legislation, with the federal government now actively seeking to preempt the latter.

## Key Findings

### EU AI Act: Binding Legal Obligations
Under Article 53, GPAI model providers must maintain technical documentation, share it with authorities and downstream providers, establish a copyright policy, and publish a summary of training data; open-source models receive partial exemptions unless classified as systemic risk (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-53), [EU Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/guidelines-obligations-general-purpose-ai-providers)). Under Article 55, providers of systemic-risk GPAI models must additionally conduct model evaluations, track and report serious incidents, and ensure adequate cybersecurity (medium confidence) ([EU Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/general-purpose-ai-models-ai-act-questions-answers)). Systemic-risk providers must notify the EU AI Office without delay of relevant incidents (medium confidence) ([EU Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/questions-and-answers-code-practice-general-purpose-ai)). The Act entered into force on 1 August 2024 (medium confidence), with GPAI provider obligations becoming applicable from 2 August 2025 (medium confidence) ([JRC](https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/bitstream/JRC143260/JRC143260_01.pdf), [EU Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-gpai-providers)).

### EU Code of Practice as Compliance Pathway
Providers who sign the voluntary GPAI Code of Practice receive streamlined compliance treatment, with Commission enforcement centered on monitoring code adherence (medium confidence) ([EU Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/ai-office-invites-providers-sign-gpai-code-practice)). On 1 August 2025, the AI Office and Board published an adequacy assessment of the final Code and invited sign-on (medium confidence) ([European Parliament](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/ATAG/2025/775890/EPRS_ATA(2025)775890_EN.pdf)). The Code's Safety and Security chapter requires systemic-risk providers to forecast when models may exceed the highest risk tier (medium confidence) ([EU Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/third-gpai-signatory-taskforce-meeting-safety-and-security-chapter)).

### US Federal Approach: Executive Orders and Voluntary Frameworks
Executive Order 14110 was rescinded in January 2025 (low confidence, contested terminology) ([regulations.ai](https://regulations.ai/regulations/RAI-US-NA-EOSSTXX-2023), [ComplyJet](https://www.complyjet.com/blog/nist-ai-risk-management-framework)). In July 2025, the Trump Administration released the non-binding "America's AI Action Plan," spanning over 90 actions across innovation, infrastructure, and diplomacy (low confidence) ([Sidley Austin](https://www.sidley.com/en/insights/newsupdates/2025/07/the-trump-administrations-2025-ai-action-plan), [White House](https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2025/07/white-house-unveils-americas-ai-action-plan)), accompanied by executive orders on AI exports, federal permitting, and "preventing woke AI" (low confidence) ([Mayer Brown](https://www.mayerbrown.com/en/insights/publications/2025/07/trump-administration-unveils-ai-action-plan-with-implications-for-innovation-infrastructure-and-global-tech-competition)). The Plan also recommended revising the NIST AI RMF to remove references to misinformation, DEI, and climate change (low confidence) ([ComplyJet](https://www.complyjet.com/blog/nist-ai-risk-management-framework)). On December 11, 2025, an Executive Order sought a uniform federal AI standard and directed legislation to preempt state AI laws, with limited exceptions like child safety (medium confidence) ([Sidley Austin](https://www.sidley.com/en/insights/newsupdates/2025/12/unpacking-the-december-11-2025-executive-order), [Moore & Van Allen](https://www.mvalaw.com/data-points/president-trump-takes-aim-at-state-artificial-intelligence-regulation-with-limited-exceptions)). A further order in June 2026 reportedly established cybersecurity mandates and a voluntary frontier-model deployment framework (low confidence) ([Lathrop GPM](https://www.lathropgpm.com/insights/new-executive-order-signals-evolving-federal-approach-to-ai)). The NIST AI RMF itself remains voluntary, continuing to be updated (e.g., agentic AI profiles) without a formal "2.0" release (low confidence) ([ComplyJet](https://www.complyjet.com/blog/nist-ai-risk-management-framework), [Cloud Security Alliance](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/agentic/agentic-nist-ai-rmf-profile-v1)).

### Structural Comparison
As of 2026, the EU enforces a horizontal, risk-tiered statute while the US combines federal executive action with a fast-moving state law patchwork rather than a unified federal statute (medium confidence) ([Collibra](https://www.collibra.com/blog/ai-regulatory-compliance-in-2026-eu-ai-act-us-orders-and-state-laws-and-how-to-operationalize), [ailawsbystate.com](https://www.ailawsbystate.com/blog/eu-ai-act-vs-us-state-ai-laws-comparison)). US federal policy relies on executive orders and voluntary frameworks rather than enacted statutory requirements specific to foundation models (medium confidence) ([CSIS](https://www.csis.org/analysis/toward-federal-framework-lessons-state-and-international-frontier-ai-regulation), [Bipartisan Policy Center](https://bipartisanpolicy.org/explainer/strategic-federal-actions-aim-to-strengthen-ai-and-energy-infrastructure)). CSIS analysis through mid-2026 finds the most pro-regulatory state frontier-AI bills have failed while more modest proposals gained traction (low confidence) ([CSIS](https://www.csis.org/analysis/toward-federal-framework-lessons-state-and-international-frontier-ai-regulation)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources disagree on whether EO 14110 was "repealed" or "rescinded," though both agree it ceased effect around January 20, 2025 ([regulations.ai](https://regulations.ai/regulations/RAI-US-NA-EOSSTXX-2023); [ComplyJet](https://www.complyjet.com/blog/nist-ai-risk-management-framework)). Several claims about US executive actions (claims 010, 011, 012, 014, 018) carry low confidence due to limited authority/recency of sources and should be treated cautiously, especially the dated June 2026 order, which rests on a single source.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source offers a provision-by-provision legal comparison of EU Article 53/55 duties against binding US requirements, since no such binding US statute exists. It remains unclear whether the December 2025 EO's preemption proposal has been enacted by Congress, what concrete penalties exist federally for US foundation model providers, how the June 2026 EO interacts with NIST AI RMF or the December 2025 EO, and which state laws would ultimately be preempted. Compute-based systemic-risk thresholds under the EU Act also lack a clear US analogue in the available sources.
